name: Generative AI, Performance, and Learning: Intervention Rank Reversal Across Assessment Regimes
headline: Generative AI, Performance, and Learning: Intervention Rank Reversal Across Assessment Regimes
abstract: Generative AI can improve performance while assistance is available without implying equivalent gains in later independent performance. This study examines whether intervention ordering can change across outcome-elicitation contexts and what can be inferred when it does. Assessment-regime rank reversal is defined as a qualitative interaction in which the direct contrast between two interventions changes sign across construct-linked assessment contexts. In Wong and Qiu's randomized creativity study, unrestricted ChatGPT exceeded learner-first AI on the assisted product-improvement task, whereas learner-first AI exceeded unrestricted ChatGPT on the subsequent unassisted product-invention task for originality and usefulness; both directional reversal tests remained significant after Holm adjustment (p=0.0068). Because task content, time, transfer demand, and AI availability changed jointly, this finding is interpreted as a regime-and-task-specific reversal on aligned creativity dimensions, not as an isolated causal effect of AI removal. Bastani and Bassner provide same-sign boundary patterns but do not meet the same evidential standard for robust population preservation. The methodological implication is that randomization identifies contrasts within observed outcome-elicitation contexts but does not guarantee a context-invariant intervention ranking. The Assessment-Regime Reporting Profile (ARRP) is proposed as an outcome-level reporting template for making these distinctions explicit; its executable implementation supports specification conformance but has not undergone independent inter-rater or content-validity evaluation.
